extraction.name: CommonCatalog
extraction.description: CommonCatalog is a dataset of approximately 70 million Creative-Commons-licensed (CC) images paired with high-quality synthetic captions generated using a pre-trained BLIP-2 model. The dataset is derived from the YFCC100M dataset, with images re-scraped from Flickr at high resolution. It is divided into two subsets: CommonCatalog-C (approximately 25 million images licensed for commercial use) and CommonCatalog-NC (approximately 70 million images licensed for non-commercial use, which includes the commercial subset). The dataset was created to train open text-to-image diffusion models (CommonCanvas) as an alternative to web-scraped datasets like LAION-2B, addressing copyright and reproducibility concerns.
extraction.creator: Aaron Gokaslan, A. Feder Cooper, Jasmine Collins, Landan Seguin, Austin Jacobson, Mihir Patel, Jonathan Frankle, Cory Stephenson, Volodymyr Kuleshov (Cornell Tech and Databricks Mosaic)
extraction.citeAs: Gokaslan, A., Cooper, A.F., Collins, J., Seguin, L., Jacobson, A., Patel, M., Frankle, J., Stephenson, C., & Kuleshov, V. (2023). CommonCanvas: An Open Diffusion Model Trained with Creative-Commons Images. arXiv:2310.16825.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Creative-Commons-licensed images were sourced starting from the YFCC100M dataset, which consists of 100 million CC-licensed images with Flickr IDs. Because the original YFCC100M images were low-resolution and had licenses not expressly allowing distribution of derivative works, the authors re-scraped the images directly from Flickr using the IDs provided in the YFCC100M metadata to obtain high-resolution versions (exceeding 4K).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: CC images rarely contain the alt-text captions necessary to train T2I models; those that do have associated text often just include the image title or a URL. This caption-data incompleteness was addressed by generating synthetic captions using BLIP-2.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Source images were obtained from Flickr via the YFCC100M dataset metadata (Flickr IDs). The authors re-scraped high-resolution versions of these Creative-Commons-licensed images directly from Flickr.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Images were center-cropped and resized to a maximum size of 512x512 pixels for the captioning process because captioning at native resolution would be very expensive. At training time of the diffusion model, all images remain in their native resolution.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were filtered by license type: non-derivative (ND) licenses were excluded from training. The remaining images were split into commercial (C) and non-commercial (NC) subsets based on license. Images were center-cropped and resized to 512x512 maximum for caption generation. VAE and text encoder latents were pre-computed over the training dataset.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Synthetic captions were generated for all YFCC100M Creative-Commons images using a pre-trained BLIP-2 OPT2.5B model. This process is described as 'telephoning' - an intuitive transfer learning technique where high-dimensional image inputs are 'lossy compressed' into short-text captions via a pre-trained vision-language model. The captioning required approximately 1,120 GPU A100 hours.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Qualitative analysis compared BLIP-2 generated captions to LAION-2B ground-truth alt-text captions, finding BLIP-2 captions were often more descriptive and better aligned with human-generated language. The authors note reduced diversity of n-grams in synthetic captions (fewer unique trigrams), a pattern previously observed by Nguyen et al. CLIP Score was used to evaluate caption-image alignment.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The CommonCatalog dataset of CC images and synthetic captions, along with trained CommonCanvas models, are released at https://github.com/mosaicml/diffusion/blob/main/assets/common-canvas.md. The authors plan to augment CommonCatalog with Creative-Commons images from other sources in the future.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset may contain images of people, faces, and celebrities/public figures (as demonstrated in experimental evaluations showing generations of public figures like Bill Gates, Elon Musk, Barack Obama, etc.). The paper does not explicitly catalog sensitive attributes collected.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The work addresses copyright concerns in training generative models by using only open-licensed Creative-Commons images with known provenance. It aims to provide a more reproducible and legally clearer alternative to web-scraped datasets like LAION-2B, which face ongoing copyright lawsuits. The paper demonstrates that CommonCanvas is less likely to generate iconic copyrighted characters (e.g., Elsa from Frozen, Snoopy) compared to SD2.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset uses YFCC100M data which is approximately a decade old; its CC images are not as current as those in LAION-2B. Synthetic captions exhibit reduced diversity of n-grams (fewer unique trigrams) compared to human-generated captions. Models trained on this data underperform in categories like faces, general photography, and paintings.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The YFCC100M source data is about a decade old and not as current as LAION-2B. Models trained on this dataset underperform in several categories including faces, general photography, and paintings. The dataset relies on synthetic captions rather than human-authored ones, which has certain performance tradeoffs. Images were center-cropped and resized to 512x512 for captioning (though training uses native resolution).
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training text-to-image (T2I) generative models, specifically latent diffusion models like CommonCanvas. The dataset is split into commercial (CommonCatalog-C) and non-commercial (CommonCatalog-NC) subsets to support different usage contexts. BLIP-2 captions for non-derivative (ND) CC images are also released as an evaluation set.
